content_preview.title: Ladybird's October Update Ships a JavaScript JIT, Rewrites Its WebAssembly Engine, and Passes Safari Technology Preview on WPT
content_preview.summary: Ladybird's October report describes a new JavaScript JIT, a Rust-based WebAssembly engine 7.3x faster on shared JetStream 3 workloads, and a Web Platform Tests score ahead of Safari Technology Preview.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Ladybird, the independent open-source browser project, published its October progress report on October 31, describing a new just-in-time (JIT) compiler for JavaScript, a rewritten WebAssembly engine, and a Web Platform Tests (WPT) score that overtook Safari Technology Preview. According to the [Ladybird newsletter](https://ladybird.org/newsletter/2026-10-31), the project also moved style and layout computation off the browser's main thread and redesigned its user interface. editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (900 words, within the 400-1200 range) covering Ladybird's October progress report: a new JavaScript JIT, a Rust-rewritten WebAssembly engine, passing Safari Technology Preview on WPT, off-main-thread style/layout, a redesigned UI, and continued Rust migration. Section headers map cleanly to the newsletter's own structure. Tone is neutral throughout; subjective project claims (e.g. 'no other browser can do this today') are explicitly flagged as Ladybird's own assertion rather than independently verified.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read all 3 snapshots from disk (gunzip -c) after confirming each file's sha256 against manifest.json (source-0: 03c6a8d2...ad772; source-1: 1fdfe360...4fc52e; source-2: 3fd16ba1...71f1e — all matched). All status_code 200, suspicious_patterns null for every source; no injection concerns. (1) source-0.html.gz = ladybird.org/newsletter/2026-10-31 (text-extracted, 10,132 chars): confirmed the JIT description and 'deliberately boring...runtime type profiling' quote, the '300ms hang into a 150ms hang' quote verbatim, the fuzzer quote verbatim, the WebAssembly engine replacement and 'about 7x higher' rounded JetStream 3 figure, the Flap/July origin statement ('In July, we built flap...for writing LibJS's interpreter'), the JSLinux 1.8s/1.5s figures, the WPT Oct 26 milestone and 2,184,722/75,650 figures, and the 'no other browser can do this today' quote verbatim. The Chrome/Firefox/Safari TP month-end subtest counts (2,244,397 / 2,189,315 / 2,172,990) and the Speedometer 2 (84->156), Speedometer 3 (5.9->8.6), Octane (4.7x) and Wasm CoreMark (2.5x) figures are not in the page's visible text but are confirmed verbatim in the descriptive alt text of the newsletter's embedded chart images (grep-verified in raw HTML), which is legitimate content of the snapshot. (2) source-1.html.gz = github.com/.../pull/12963 (41,941 chars extracted): confirmed merge date Oct 22, 2026; confirmed the Rust engine/Flap interpreter/own JIT description; confirmed 'One Flap source builds the interpreter for x86-64, AArch64 and Windows x64' verbatim; confirmed 'JetStream 3's 19 WebAssembly workloads all run; the old engine fails 8 of them. On the 11 both run, the new engine scores 7.3x higher (geometric mean)' verbatim, matching the article's precise figure exactly. Confirmed this PR does NOT state a July origin for Flap (only that the interpreter 'is written in Flap, the language LibJS's interpreter is written in') -- the article correctly sources the July-origin claim to the newsletter, not to this PR. (3) source-2.html.gz = github.com/.../pull/12613 (9,628 chars extracted): confirmed merge date Oct 11, 2026, title 'LibJS: Turn the JIT on by default', and the LIBJS_JIT=off environment-variable override described in the PR body -- matches the article's 'turned the JIT on by default...with an environment variable available to disable it' exactly. Anthropic disclosure: not required - article subject is the Ladybird browser project; no mention of Anthropic, Claude, Claude Code or Bun in the body.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Quote-by-quote audit: every direct quotation in the body (the 300ms/150ms hang line, the 'deliberately boring' design description, the fuzzer-comparison line, and the 'no other browser can do this today' line) appears verbatim in the newsletter snapshot -- no paraphrase-as-quote found. Figure-attribution check requested by the orchestrator: the newsletter's rounded 'about 7x higher' and the PR's precise '7.3x higher (geometric mean)' both describe the same 11 JetStream 3 workloads both engines complete, and the article attributes each figure to its correct, distinct source ('The newsletter says...about 7x higher. The pull request itself is more specific...scored 7.3 times higher') -- no conflation. Flap July-origin check: confirmed the July-origin claim is sourced solely to the newsletter ('a language the newsletter said the project built in July'), not to PR #12963, which never states when Flap was created -- the article's attribution is correct as written. Derived/vendor figures (8 of 19 workloads failed by the old engine, 11 shared workloads, geometric mean) recomputed directly from PR #12963's own prose and benchmark table and match. Quantifier/absence language in the body ('both engines could complete', 'no other browser can do this today', 'first alpha release') checked against both snapshots: all supported and correctly scoped (the 'no other browser' claim is explicitly framed as Ladybird's own, unverified assertion, not stated as fact).
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and attributive throughout; every benchmark and milestone claim is explicitly sourced to 'the newsletter' or 'the pull request' rather than stated as established fact, including an explicit editorial caveat that the WPT ranking and the main-thread-concurrency claim come solely from Ladybird's own report.
editor_notes.originality: Genuine follow-up, not a duplicate. Only one prior Ladybird article exists in the archive (src/content/articles/2026-10/08-ladybirds-september-update-...-trail-of-bits.md, covering the September report: Trail of Bits security testing, macOS hardware video decoding, a separate media process). That article covers entirely different subject matter from this October-report submission (JS JIT, WebAssembly rewrite, WPT ranking). The body's internal link to the September article (/article/2026-10/08-ladybirds-september-update-...) resolves to that exact file -- correct singular '/article/' form, not the paginated '/articles/' listing route.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Clean, well-verified News submission: every direct quote checked verbatim against the newsletter snapshot, the newsletter-vs-PR WASM speedup figures (rounded ~7x vs. precise 7.3x) are correctly attributed to their respective sources with no conflation, the Flap language's July origin is correctly sourced to the newsletter rather than misattributed to the PR, and the piece is a genuine distinct follow-up to the Herald's existing September Ladybird coverage. No corrections needed. Featured candidacy: 1 - a well-sourced, technically substantive monthly progress report (a from-scratch JS JIT and a full Rust WebAssembly rewrite are real engineering milestones) but routine recurring coverage for a browser-development audience rather than broad-interest news.
